title: Psalm 31: Into Your Hands
summary: A man hunted by enemies, wasted by grief, and abandoned by friends entrusts himself to the LORD, his rock and refuge. Twice the psalm moves from distress to trust, and it ends by praising God's goodness and urging all the faithful to be strong and to hope in the LORD.
story: Psalm 30 celebrated rescue after the fact. Psalm 31 lives in the middle of trouble, where rescue is prayed for, glimpsed, and then prayed for again. It belongs to the many laments of Book I of the Psalter, most of them attributed to David, and it gives voice to someone who is both hunted and ashamed, sick and slandered. Its most famous line, the prayer of verse 5 committing one's spirit into God's hands, became the dying prayer of Jesus, and through him the evening prayer of the church for centuries. The psalm teaches a reader that trust in God is not a single decision but a return, made again each time fear comes back.
historical:
The heading names the choirmaster, probably the leader of the temple music, and attributes the psalm to David. No specific event is named. Verse 21 speaks of God's loving devotion shown in a city under siege, which some readers connect with David's time at Keilah, a town he rescued and then had to flee because its people would have handed him to Saul (1 Samuel 23:1-13). Others take the siege as a metaphor for being hemmed in on every side. As with most psalm headings, scholars disagree about whether David himself wrote the poem or whether the heading places it in a Davidic collection; the psalm's language is general enough that many different sufferers could pray it.

The phrase terror on every side in verse 13 appears repeatedly in the prophet Jeremiah (for example Jeremiah 6:25 and 20:10), where it describes the menace closing around him in Jerusalem around 600 BC. Some scholars think Jeremiah borrowed it from this psalm; others think both drew on a common expression. Either way, the words gave later sufferers a way to name the panic of being surrounded.
cultural:
Several images come from the physical world of Israel. The rock and fortress of verses 2 and 3 are the high crags and hilltop strongholds of Judah's wilderness, where David hid from Saul. The net of verse 4 is a hunter's trap for birds. The broken vessel of verse 12 is a clay pot, the most ordinary household object, which once cracked was useless and thrown on a heap. To be like a broken pot and forgotten like a dead man was to be discarded by the community.

The psalm also reflects a culture of honor and shame. Being put to shame (verses 1 and 17) was not only an inner feeling but public disgrace, the collapse of one's standing before neighbors. The speaker's friends avoid him in the street, perhaps because his suffering was read as a sign of God's disfavor. To say my times are in Your hands (verse 15) was to hand the whole course of one's life, its seasons and its end, to God rather than to the enemies who plotted to cut it short.
literary: The psalm moves in two waves. Verses 1 to 8 open with a plea and turn to confident trust. Verses 9 to 18 go back down into distress, more personal and more painful, before turning again to trust at verse 14 with the word But. Verses 19 to 24 then open into praise and end by addressing the whole congregation. Refuge vocabulary threads through the poem (verses 1, 2, 4, 19), as do hands: God's hands receive the speaker's spirit in verse 5 and hold his times in verse 15, while the enemy's hand is what he is spared from in verse 8. Verse 22 quotes the speaker's own panic, I am cut off from Your sight, and then answers it with the fact that God heard.

outline.t: Refuge in God, the rock and fortress; the spirit committed
Trust in the LORD rather than worthless idols
Grief, weakness, and the scorn of neighbors and friends
My times are in Your hands: a renewed plea
The goodness God stores up for those who take refuge in him
A call to the faithful to love the LORD and take courage

doctrines.note: Faith in this psalm is entrusting oneself, body, life, and future, into God's hands. It is not the absence of fear; the speaker trusts, falls back into anguish, and trusts again. The repeated turn to You are my God shows faith as a practiced return.
My times are in Your hands confesses that the seasons of a life and its length rest with God, not with enemies or circumstance. That confession frees the speaker to pray honestly without despair.

The psalm gives unusually full voice to the social pain of suffering: shame, gossip, friends crossing the street. It also admits that iniquity has played a part (verse 10), without reducing all the suffering to punishment.

words.note: Paqad, here to commit or entrust. The verb has a wide range: to visit, to muster, to appoint, to put in someone's charge. In verse 5 it means handing something over for safekeeping, as one deposits a valuable with a trusted guardian. That sense gives the dying prayer of Jesus its weight: not resignation, but deposit.

Chasah, to take refuge. It pictures running to a shelter from a storm or an enemy. It opens the psalm (verse 1) and returns in verse 19, where God's goodness is stored up for those who take refuge in him. In the Psalms it is one of the most common words for trust.

Chesed, rendered loving devotion in the BSB, is the steady, loyal love that God has pledged to his covenant people. It appears three times here (verses 7, 16, and 21). It is love that keeps its promises, and the psalmist appeals to it as the ground of his rescue rather than to his own merit.

christ: Luke records that Jesus, dying on the cross, cried with a loud voice and quoted this psalm, committing his spirit into his Father's hands (Luke 23:46). The psalm was a trusting prayer long before the cross, but in Jesus' mouth it becomes the prayer of the innocent sufferer who gives his life rather than having it taken from him, and whose trust is vindicated three days later. Stephen prayed a similar prayer to Jesus himself as he died (Acts 7:59), which shows how quickly the first Christians made this psalm their own. Other lines fit the pattern of Christ's suffering as well: the scorn of neighbors, friends who flee, enemies who plot to take his life. Those echoes are thematic rather than predictive, but the New Testament treats the righteous sufferer of the Psalms as a figure whom Jesus fulfills.
questions: What would it look like, in a concrete situation you are facing, to say my times are in Your hands?
The speaker turns from fear to trust and then falls back into anguish. Why do you think the psalm leaves that back-and-forth in place rather than smoothing it out?
Verse 11 describes friends who avoid a suffering person. Who around you might feel like a broken vessel, and how could you draw near?
